blocks.content: Compose offers a few different ways to work with environment variables, setting them per service directly, loading them from a file, and even using them to substitute values inside the Compose file itself.
1. Setting Variables Directly on a Service
blocks.text: 1. Setting Variables Directly on a Service

blocks.content: The simplest approach, an environment block inside a service, lists variables directly, exactly equivalent to a series of -e flags on docker run, just declared in the file instead.

blocks.alt: Variables listed directly in the service definition

blocks.content:
services:
  app:
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      PORT: 3000

code.content:
services:
  app:
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      PORT: 3000

codes.yaml:
services:
  app:
    environment:
      NODE_ENV: production
      PORT: 3000

blocks.content: 2. Loading a Whole File per Service
blocks.text: 2. Loading a Whole File per Service

blocks.content: For a larger set of variables, env_file points a service at a file to load in bulk, the same .env file format and --env-file mechanics covered in the Environment Variables module, applied per service instead of at the command line.

blocks.alt: A whole file of variables, loaded for just this service

blocks.content: 3. Substituting Values Inside the Compose File Itself
blocks.text: 3. Substituting Values Inside the Compose File Itself

blocks.content: This is a distinct, easily confused mechanism: a .env file sitting at the project root (next to docker-compose.yml) is used by Compose to substitute $VARIABLE references written directly inside the YAML file itself, before the file is even parsed as a stack definition.

blocks.alt: A .env file feeding values into the Compose file's own syntax

blocks.content:
# .env, at the project root
IMAGE_TAG=1.4.2

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    image: myapp:${IMAGE_TAG}

code.content:
# .env, at the project root
IMAGE_TAG=1.4.2

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    image: myapp:${IMAGE_TAG}

codes.yaml:
# .env, at the project root
IMAGE_TAG=1.4.2

# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    image: myapp:${IMAGE_TAG}

blocks.content: It is worth being precise about the distinction: variables set via environment or env_file end up inside the running container, available to your application. The root .env file's substitution happens in the Compose YAML itself, before any container even exists, they can overlap in name but serve entirely different purposes.

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: environment and env_file set variables inside a running service's container, exactly like -e or --env-file on docker run.
A root-level .env file is a separate mechanism, substituting $VARIABLE values directly into the Compose YAML before the stack is even built.
